UK project Vauxhall Residences in Liverpool to launch for sale, prices from GBP195,000
article:
Vauxhall Residences, a new residential development in Liverpool, UK, will launch for sale in Singapore during the weekend of Oct 3 and 4.

The project is located in Pumpfields, an emerging district at the northern edge of Liverpool’s city centre. It offers 158 units of one- and two-bedroom apartments, along with two- and three-bedroom townhouses.

Savills Singapore is marketing the properties. According to the firm, prices for the homes start from:

GBP195,000 (about $330,000) for a one-bedder GBP 288,500 for a two-bedder GBP 280,000 for a two-bed townhouse GBP335,000 for a three-bed townhouse

The development will include amenities such as a gym, co-working space, a cafe and rooftop gardens. It is expected to be completed in 4Q2028.

It is 600m away from the Moorfields railway station and 1.3km away from Liverpool Lime Street Station, a major transportation hub with direct services to London, Manchester and other cities.

Pumpfields is a 75-acre (30ha) regeneration zone that will see the former industrial district redeveloped into a mixed-use neighbourhood with new residential, commercial and community spaces. It is part of a wider transformation of Liverpool’s historic northern docks.

The rejuvenated Pumpfields district is slated to deliver over 7,000 new homes, alongside an urban park, public squares, green corridors and improved connections to the waterfront.

Vauxhall Residences is a project by Rosmara Development Group, a Manchester-based developer.

Adrian Lim, senior director and head of international residential sales at Savills Singapore, notes that Liverpool is compelling to Singapore buyers looking at UK property.

“It is a globally recognised city with a strong cultural identity, a large student population and an established business base, while significant regeneration is creating new neighbourhoods and opportunities beyond its traditional city centre,” he explained.

Vauxhall Residences’ proximity to the Liverpool city centre, along with the ongoing rejuvenation of Pumpfields and the wider district, makes the project "particularly interesting for buyers taking a longer-term view", Lim added.

Savills will be holding a launch event for Vauxhall Residences on Oct 3 and 4 at Voco Orchard Hotel, from 2pm to 6pm.

title: Hilton brings Motto brand to Japan with 108-room Kyoto hotel opening in 2029
article:
Hilton is partnering with Heiwa Real Estate Co to open Motto by Hilton Kyoto Shijo Karasuma. The 108-key hotel will open in 2029.

This will be the first Motto by Hilton property in Japan. The hotel will include an all-day dining restaurant and a lounge with an open terrace.

“Motto by Hilton Kyoto Shijo Karasuma will offer a fresh, locally rooted hospitality experience that encourages gathering, creating a new type of stay for guests looking to immerse themselves in Japan's cultural capital,” said Alex Shockley, Hilton’ senior director, lifestyle and collection brands for Asia Pacific.

Hilton will manage the property for Heiwa. The Japanese developer and real estate company manages a portfolio of commercial and residential properties in Japan, including the stock exchange buildings in cities such as Tokyo, Osaka, Nagoya and Fukuoka.

“As part of our efforts to realise our long-term vision, WAY2040, we are expanding our hotel business as a new area of growth,” said Kiyoyuki Tsuchimoto, the company’s representative executive officer, president and CEO.

The hotel will be a two-minute walk from Shijo Station on the Kyoto Municipal Subway Karasuma Line and Karasuma Station on the Hankyu Kyoto Line. This will allow guests convenient transport access to popular Kyoto attractions such as Nishiki Market, the historic Gion and Higashiyama districts, and retail offerings in the Shijo Kawaramachi area.

Hilton currently operates 13 Motto hotels, with over 24 hotels under development. Recent openings included properties in Brazil and Nashville, USA, while the group has also inked agreements for properties in Paris, Shanghai and Sydney.

In Kyoto, Hilton’s portfolio is set to grow to seven hotels across various brands, including an upcoming Curio Collection by Hilton property.

title: 3 Singapore Stocks Quietly Profiting From The AI Boom
article:
The most compelling semiconductor plays tend to be
global names
such as
NVIDIA Corporation
(NASDAQ: NVDA) and
Micron Technology, Inc.
(NASDAQ: MU).
While Singapore does not mint such global tech giants, the small city-state still holds its own, being home to precision engineering and technology companies that play crucial roles in the global
semiconductor supply chain
.
Instead of designing artificial intelligence (AI) chips or building frontier language models, these AI enablers supply specialised testing equipment, precision front-end equipment components, and essential consumable tools for global chipmakers.
To sweeten the deal for local investors, these companies –
AEM Holdings Ltd.
(SGX: AWX),
UMS Integration Limited
(SGX: 558), and
Micro-Mechanics (Holdings) Ltd.
(SGX: 5DD) – pay tax-free dividends on top of potential capital appreciation.
AEM Holdings: Testing the Next Generation of AI Chips
AI processors are becoming more powerful.
But that power comes with a hefty operational cost: extreme heat generation.
While the complex designs of AI chips make them powerful, they also make them vulnerable to this intense heat.
Given this vulnerability, stress testing of costly AI chips under real-world operating conditions is more crucial than ever.
To this end, AEM’s PiXL technology fills the thermal integrity gap, offering precise thermal testing at scale to ensure high-powered AI chips can perform reliably under extreme conditions.
Strategically, it expands with a “Razor/Razorblade” model that generates recurring sales.
Crucially, analysts believe the
collaboration
between
Intel Corporation
(NASDAQ: INTC) and NVIDIA could lift demand for AEM’s testing solutions, though the benefit may only show up in the medium term.
Management has raised its FY2026 revenue guidance to between S$630 million to S$680 million, up from between S$550 million to S$600 million.
AEM’s group revenue for the first half of 2026 (1H2026) climbed 29.9% year on year (YoY) to S$247.2 million, while its net profit rose 875.6% YoY to S$30.8 million, driven by higher demand from its fabless AI/HPC customer.
Furthermore, the group’s partnership with
ASE Technology
(NYSE: ASX), a major outsourced semiconductor assembly and test (OSAT) provider, could help AEM tap demand from hyperscalers.
With a net cash position of S$56.6 million and a low debt-to-equity ratio of 0.05x, AEM’s strong balance sheet supports a 1H2026 interim dividend of S$0.024 per share, following a final dividend of S$0.013 per share for FY2025.
UMS Integration: The Front-End Precision Powerhouse
While AEM anchors the growth in back-end AI testing, UMS offers a front-end equipment play.
UMS has long provided precision component manufacturing and electromechanical assembly for front-end chipmaking equipment to
Applied Materials
(NASDAQ: AMAT), one of the world’s largest semiconductor equipment makers and its key customer.
Crucially, UMS has also onboarded another major semiconductor equipment maker as a customer, which is starting to reduce its reliance on a single client.
In the second quarter of 2026 (2Q2026), UMS’s revenue jumped 29% YoY to S$87.1 million, driving net profit up 90% to S$19.8 million, as initial contributions from this new customer ramped up, alongside increased contributions from existing customers and aerospace demand.
Notably, the company operates with net cash of S$38.6 million on its balance sheet as at 30 June 2026, with no bank borrowings, and declared a 2Q2026 interim dividend of S$0.010 per share, unchanged YoY.
Micro-Mechanics: The High-Margin Consumable Cash Machine
AI-linked equipment makers potentially face inconsistent revenue due to customers’ lumpy investment cycles.
Micro-Mechanics is less exposed to these swings.
Instead of selling costly one-off equipment, it provides high-precision, miniature consumable tools, such as die-attach and wire-bonding tools, that eventually wear out as chips are assembled and tested, sustaining recurring demand.
As global chip production rises, so does demand for these high-precision, complementary tools, which benefits Micro-Mechanics.
Additionally, by serving over 600 global customers through its localised manufacturing facilities, the company is cushioned against geopolitical friction.
In the fiscal year ended 30 June 2026 (FY2026), Micro-Mechanics’ revenue rose 15.8% to S$75.5 million on strong demand for its consumable tools, while operating cash flow edged up 3.5% to S$18.9 million.
To sweeten the deal for investors, the company has no debt, boasts a net cash position of S$30.1 million, and rewards shareholders with a total dividend of S$0.06 per share (unchanged YoY).
This includes a proposed S$0.03 final dividend, subject to shareholder approval at its annual general meeting on 26 October 2026.
Get Smart: Riding the AI Boom with Local Names
Here’s the thing about riding the
AI boom
: You don’t necessarily need to chase expensive US tech giants.
Local AI enablers like AEM, UMS, and Micro-Mechanics offer a way to gain exposure to three parts of the AI chip supply chain: testing, front-end manufacturing and consumable tools.
Beyond growing market demand, this AI-enabling trio boasts solid balance sheets and robust profitability.
Crucially, all three pay tax-free dividends, adding a stream of income for Singapore investors on top of any business growth.
Not all AI “winners” will survive this cycle.

title: Global cash funding US AI boom despite fears of hidden debt
article:
(Sept 30): Foreign investors are increasingly funding the growth of artificial intelligence computing across North America, JPMorgan Asset Management’s Charles Wu told an audience at the SuperReturn conference in Singapore on Wednesday.

Foreign banks and institutional investors including pensions, sovereign wealth funds and insurance companies from regions including Asia and the Gulf are playing a major part in funding the expansion of a sector where capital expenditure stands at almost US$1 trillion ($1.3 trillion), said Wu, the bank’s head of Asia-Pacific alternatives institutional client strategy.

“Compute training assets are still largely in North America,” he said on a panel. “On the banking side and also on the asset management side, the capital providing the funding for these assets is largely becoming more global.”

How global investors approach the AI trade — including the mammoth funding needs for the world’s data centres — has been a key topic of conversation at the SuperReturn event this week. Most panelists have struck a positive tone, but there are also detectable notes of caution.

“We’re being very careful with the way we assess the risk,” said Jean-Christophe Aubert, a senior director of infrastructure investments at PSP Investments. “Concentration is a big point, but also for us, given the amount of capital that we would have to put to work, is trying to understand how can we ultimately realise those assets going forward.”

While US hyperscalers are funding much of the AI capex need through operating cash flows, they are also getting about US$250 billion from the bond market and roughly the same amount from bank loans, said Wu. He warned that his firm was keeping an eye on concerns including lease commitments and concentration risk, as well as the risk that some of the financing is being raised off balance sheet.

See also: Apple will sell six million iPhone Duos in 2026, Counterpoint says

“The reality is a lot of these funding securities, whether you’re talking about investment-grade bonds, 144a, private placements, even private credit structured deals — a lot of them seem to all triangulate to basically five key hyperscaler parties,” he said. “Either as a guarantor, as a tenant, as a funding source, or as a customer.”

While the US remains the dominant market, several of the panelists agreed that Asia is likely to be close behind. The nature of inference — the actual use of AI models — benefits from being close to end users, which will help drive huge demand for infrastructure in the region.

“Asia is equally important as it plays an interesting role in both the demand side of the equation and the supply side through the physical stuff,” said Mohsin Pirzada, head of funds at Qatar Investment Authority. “What we’re starting to see is a decentralisation, and that’s being driven by end consumer demand” as well as data sovereignty and security, he said.

See also: AI faces US$6 tril test to justify data centres, Bain says

The panellists also agreed that energy remains a major bottleneck for a variety of reasons. With gas being a go-to power source, a shortage of gas turbines is causing challenges for data centres trying to scale. I Squared fund partner Chenhua Shen said Asia’s power markets were less liberalised, making access to utilities harder.

“It becomes a major obstacle for Asia to leapfrog,” she said. “But we are still very optimistic in a way because Asia enjoys very abundant renewables.”

title: BMW plans margin rebuild with simpler line-up and pricier cars
article:
(Sept 30): BMW AG plans to restore margins by simplifying its business, cutting costs and selling more expensive cars, according to Bernstein analysts who took part in the company’s capital markets day.

The German automaker is trying to rebuild profitability after China’s ongoing price war and heavy spending on its electric-car overhaul squeezed returns. Management is aiming to lift auto margins to 3% to 5% by 2028 and to its long-term target range of 8% to 10% early next decade, Bernstein analyst Stephen Reitman wrote on Wednesday in a note.

BMW executives briefed analysts and investors on Tuesday and will publish the updated financial goals later on Wednesday on the second and final day of the CMD in Munich.

The mid-term targets are “disappointing”, Bloomberg Intelligence senior industry analyst Michael Dean wrote in a note. Reaching the goal of an 8% to 10% auto margin “has been pushed further out”, with few details on how it will be achieved, Dean added.

BMW had until recently stood out as the most resilient of Germany’s car manufacturers, helped by a flexible electric-vehicle strategy and a premium-heavy line-up. That distinction vanished with a major profit warning in June, as China’s deepening slump, fierce local competition and the huge cost of electrification hammered margins.

BMW and its European peers are facing stiff competition from upstart Chinese manufacturers at home, while also suffering steep declines in sales in China, the world’s biggest market. That has deprived them of a lucrative revenue stream they relied on for years.

See also: McLaren reveals a new visual identity for automotive and racing

BMW chief executive officer Milan Nedeljkovic’s challenge is to claw back returns while still funding the technology and new models BMW needs to stay competitive. Among his first steps was cutting jobs by around 8,000, just over 5% of its workforce.

“BMW’s financial message is that 2026 is a transition year, with profitability expected to recover in stages,” Reitman wrote. Bernstein rates BMW outperform with an EUR82 ($119) price target. After closing at EUR54.50 on Tuesday, the shares rose as much as 1.8% in Frankfurt on Wednesday. They are down about 40% this year.

The first leg of the firm’s recovery is simplification. BMW wants to pare back an offering it concedes has become too complex, shorten development times and deepen supplier partnerships.

See also: Denza B5 Zenith arrives in Singapore

In China, it is also shrinking its dealer network and sourcing more standardised local components, which could cut the cost of those parts by 20% to 30%, Bernstein said, citing chief financial officer Walter Mertl.

BMW’s plans for higher returns via cost-cutting risk falling short as the sector goes through a fundamental shift, according to Citigroup analysts.

“Investor sentiment is clearly concerned with a much more structural industry deterioration, which would in turn require a much more structural BMW response,” they wrote. Citi has a neutral rating on BMW with a target price of EUR64.

The Munich-based firm is betting that more expensive, higher-margin models can help lift profits. It’s planning a new sport utility vehicle above the X7, its current flagship in the segment, more high-performance M cars and a bigger role for Alpina, the marque it is positioning between its mainstream luxury range and Rolls-Royce.

Its new generation of electric cars is another pillar of the recovery, with European orders for the iX3 already topping 100,000, Bernstein said.

title: Temasek to expand presence in Middle East including opening offices in Riyadh and Abu Dhabi
article:
Temasek intends to deepen its presence in the Middle East, which includes establishing offices in Riyadh, Kingdom of Saudi Arabia and Abu Dhabi in the United Arab Emirates.

The new offices will serve as “strategic hubs” for Temasek and its portfolio companies, some of which plan to co-locate in these hubs.

In its Sept 30 statement, Temasek says it also plans to “actively engage” with institutions in Qatar and other markets in the Mdidle East to “pursue partnership and investment opportunities”.

The move comes as Temasek sees “significant long-term opportunities” for itself and its portfolio companies in the region, which is undergoing a broad-based economic transformation on the back of “ambitious national development and diversification plans”.

“The Middle East is an important part of Temasek’s global network. The pace and ambition of economic transformation across the region are remarkable, and its long-term fundamentals remain highly attractive,” says Temasek Holdings’ CEO Dilhan Pillay Sandrasegara.

“We see strong alignment between the region’s priorities and Temasek’s own areas of focus. Our relationships across the Middle East – particularly in Saudi Arabia, the United Arab Emirates, and Qatar – have been built over many years through our partnerships, co-investments, and portfolio companies, and we look forward to deepening them further,” he adds. “This expansion is a natural next step, and it will help us create compelling partnerships to grow together.”

See also: Singapore doubles down on a baby push that keeps falling short

Chia Song Hwee, CEO of Temasek Global Investments and chairman of the group’s Middle East & Africa operations notes that being on the ground in the Middle East will “strengthen engagement with our partners and enhance access to investment opportunities for Temasek and our portfolio companies throughout the region and beyond to Central Asia and Africa.”

“Equally, it allows us to bring complementary expertise from across our ecosystem to these markets, expanding pathways to create lasting value with like-minded partners,” adds Chia, who was appointed chairman of the Middle East & Africa operations from Sept 1. Chia will provide senior leadership and oversight of Temasek’s engagement and long-term growth in these markets while Ankit Khemka, managing director for the region, will continue to drive the group’s strategy and expansion.

The new offices in Riyadh and Abu Dhabi are expected to be operational in the first half of 2027, subject to obtaining relevant statutory approvals. The additions will bring Temasek’s global network to 15 offices across 11 countries.

title: US fund accuses trader Radiant World of fraud in Swiss complaint
article:
(Sept 30): A US fund has filed a criminal complaint in Switzerland accusing Radiant World and related companies of fraud and money laundering, according to a US court filing, adding a new jurisdiction to the iron ore trader’s escalating legal and financial crisis.

The complaint was described in an application filed by Mariner Atlantic Multi-Strategy LLC, which is managed by investment firm Mariner Investment Group. Mariner is seeking documents from the Federal Reserve Bank of New York and the Clearing House Interbank Payments System for use in the Swiss proceedings.

In the US court papers, lawyers for Mariner said the firm entered into agreements with Radiant World under which it provided two revolving credit facilities totalling US$50 million ($63.84 million) to finance certain metals trades.

“However, after the funds were released, Mariner learned that Radiant systematically had falsified commercial documents in order to simulate transactions and thereby obtain financing from international lenders, including Mariner, through fictitious trades,” Mariner said in the Sept 29 filing.

Mariner said it has been unable to recover any of the money it transferred to Radiant, and is now seeking wire transfer and payment message records relating to Radiant group entities, according to the court papers.

The Swiss complaint, which was filed with the Geneva Public Prosecutor’s Office on Sept 14, also names Sapphire Minmetals Corporation SA, along with Radiant World’s local subsidiary and Radiant World founder Pinkesh Nahar. Mariner has asked prosecutors to open a criminal investigation, conduct searches of the premises in Geneva and seize bank accounts and other assets in Switzerland, according to the US filing.

See also: Radiant World cuts more jobs after founder loses control of firm — Bloomberg

A Radiant World spokesperson did not immediately respond to requests for comment. The company has denied wrongdoing. Mariner didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment in the US after business hours.

Guillaume Tattevin, Mariner’s lawyer, wasn’t immediately available to comment. Asked about the complaint, a spokesman for the Geneva prosecutor’s office declined to comment.

Radiant World is facing a spate of civil lawsuits from Singapore to London over allegations from creditors that it provided banks with falsified documents to secure financing, while Singapore Police are also conducting an investigation into the company. The company’s main offices are located in Singapore, Switzerland and Dubai.

See also: Copper edges higher after Chile mine union rejects pay offer

Last week, a Singapore court appointed KPMG restructuring executives to take charge of Radiant World’s operations, granting an application by creditor Mizuho Bank Ltd, which has accused the trader of fraud.

title: Burnham takes on pensions and Brexit in sweeping change agenda
article:
(Sept 30): Prime Minister Andy Burnham vowed to reopen some of the UK’s most vexing debates, from Brexit to pensions to the electoral system, in a sweeping and at times tearful call for change that resets British politics.

Burnham laid out the agenda in a speech to the Labour Party’s annual conference in Liverpool that sought to counter critics who accused him of prioritising style over substance. Instead, he promised a “new economy and a new politics”, pledging to curb the soaring cost of pensions, repeal the Thatcher-era ban on public ownership of water companies and explore options for a closer relationship with the European Union (EU).

“I will make a break with the direction of the past 40 years,” he said on stage at the Labour Party’s annual conference at Liverpool, taking aim at a loss of “control” over the UK’s borders and public services, which he blamed on Brexit and privatisation.

Burnham made no mention of his chief political rival, Reform UK’s Nigel Farage, in a speech that instead attempted to offer a state-driven antidote to the right-wing populism that’s frayed the UK’s two-party system. The only political opponent he mentioned by name was the separatist Scottish National Party’s First Minister John Swinney, who he recollected threatening recently that Burnham would be the last prime minister of a united kingdom.

The prime minister hit back in an emotional retort, in which he invoked his the aspirations of his father, who died two weeks ago. Burnham said he would instead be “the first to rewire it to make it work for all people and places, driving power out of Whitehall and into every postcode of Wales, Scotland, Northern Ireland”.

The gilt market had a limited reaction to Burnham’s address. While yields on longer-term government bonds rose slightly from the day’s lows, the moves were driven more by a rise in US Treasury yields. At 5.38%, benchmark UK 10-year yields were four basis points lower on the day.

See also: Burnham says Britain could rejoin EU after next election

UK swap spreads, which measure the difference between UK government bond yields and risk-free rates and act as a proxy for sentiment about UK fiscal risk, were little changed.

“Gilts should find comfort in Burnham’s Labour conference speech today (Tuesday), but external forces continue to be the bigger force,” said Michiel Tukker, a rates strategist at ING Bank. “Plans to reform the pension triple lock shows a dedication to fiscal credibility and a willingness to review difficult and controversial topics. Meanwhile, no obvious inflationary policies were presented.”

The centrepiece of Burnham’s new plan was a pledge to build a new National Care Service, modeled on the country’s National Health Service, which is free at the point of use. He explained that his government would change the mechanism by which pension payments are increased, to help pay for the plan.

See also: UK mortgage approvals fall to 32-month low as loan costs bite

He vowed not to fund the change through an increase in borrowing, which has soared in recent decades.

The so-called pensions triple lock has been in place since 2011, and guarantees that the benefit rises annually by the highest of inflation, wage growth or 2.5%. It’s helped to reduce pensioner poverty, but many economists warned the policy is increasingly unaffordable given other pressures on the public purse.

The move opened him up to criticism from both right-wing opponents and the left-wing of his own party. “I doubt it will save that much, but it’s such a gift to Reform,” John McDonnell, a former shadow chancellor under Jeremy Corbyn, told Bloomberg. “There are so many alternatives to funding social care without cutting pensions. It’s a pity this was included as it has spoiled a good speech.”

Farage, the leader of Reform, tweeted simply: “I will cut foreign aid, migrant welfare, welfare fraud, and mad net zero spending. Andy Burnham will cut your pension.”

In his speech to Labour, the prime minister vowed to bring water, energy and housing under greater public control. He told the party’s annual gathering that he would “break the mold” and tackle issues his predecessors had failed to address. To that end he pledged to repeal the ban on public ownership of water companies instituted in the 1980s.

“We rely on them, we pay for them, and once again we will have power over them,” Burnham said. He said regional mayors would have new powers to hold water companies to account, that loopholes used to pay bosses “excessive bonuses” would be closed, and that there would be “tougher consequences” for firms which “repeatedly fail”.

To stay ahead of Singapore and the region’s corporate and economic trends, click here for Latest Section

But he rejected the criticism that it was anti-business. “It’s the opposite. Businesses need the basics to be functional and affordable too, as does the wider economy.” Aiming most of his ambitions at the longer-term, the prime minister steered clear of revealing anything about the budget that’s taking place in a month’s time, and which has the City of London wary about potential tax increases that could target banks and capital gains.

Burnham used his speech to argue Brexit had done more harm than good to the UK, and hinted he wants the country to move closer to the EU.

At a UK-EU summit planned for later this year, Burnham said he would “lay out to the country what I believe the different options are for Britain’s long-term relationship with our European partners”, and said he would seek to find consensus about the best path forward.

Ahead of his appearance, Burnham was seeking to move away from the cheaper, feel-good policies that have characterised his first two months in office and flesh out his longer-term vision for tackling some of the biggest challenges facing the UK, in a bid to turn the page on the country’s political instability.

He said he is prepared to take political risks, even if it meant harming his own career, to do so and said he wouldn’t shy away from “the things politicians usually avoid”.

“I would love to go quicker, but I have to be honest about what the country can afford. I will stick to our fiscal rules, to get our borrowing and debt down,” he said, a day after his Chancellor of the Exchequer John Healey vowed fiscal discipline.

Burnham said he wants to take on the thorny topic of electoral reform, something historically avoided by the main parties who could lose out from changing the voting system to favour a proportional representation approach.

His senior ministers, including Healey, used their conference appearances this week to roll the pitch for more difficult decisions to come, including plans to cut spending on benefits for working-age Britons. Labour rebels forced Burnham’s predecessor Keir Starmer into a damaging U-turn last year on relatively modest plans to trim spending.

“If you agree with enough of what I’ve said, get behind this plan and get behind each other,” Burnham told his party. “It’s time to draw a line, to move beyond a decade of drift and division, to bring a spirit of unity and positivity back to our country.”

title: Burnham says Britain could rejoin EU after next election
article:
(Sept 30): UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham said he could campaign to take Britain back into the European Union (EU) at the next general election, reopening the country’s debate on its relationship with the continent a decade on from the Brexit vote.

Burnham outlined three options he would discuss at a UK-EU summit slated for later this year. One is rejoining the EU, one is rejoining the bloc’s single market, and another is entering a customs union, he told the BBC in an interview aired on Wednesday morning.

“We could stay as we are, that’s definitely an option, if people think this is the right place to stay,” the prime minister said. “We could look at what George Osborne has said about a customs union,” he added, referring to the former Conservative chancellor of the exchequer. “We could look at what the Liberal Democrats said at their conference about the single market. Or we could go all the way.”

Burnham’s remarks are the first time since the exit referendum a decade ago that a UK prime minister has suggested they could try to take the country back into the EU. He argued in his keynote speech at Labour’s annual conference on Tuesday that Brexit wasn’t working for Britain, but his comments on Wednesday went further.

He has stressed he will keep to the current Labour campaign manifesto during this Parliament, which binds him to staying outside the single market and customs union. However, he said in his speech that he wants to determine a new path for Britain’s relations with the EU at a summit later this year and then make the case for it at the next general election, which he has said will be in 2029.

title: Yen strengthens past 157 per dollar, outperforming G-10 peers
article:
(Sept 30): The yen outperformed all its Group-of-10 peers on Wednesday as a series of government warnings on the currency and quarter-end flows provided support.

Japan’s currency strengthened as much as 0.6% to 156.38 before paring some of the gains and trading at 156.97 at 3.45pm local time. It also rose as much as 0.6% against the euro and 0.9% against the Australian dollar.

Atsushi Mimura, Japan’s top currency official, told Reuters on Monday that the country’s prime minister and finance minister, along with the US, have recently sent a “very clear” message about FX depreciation. Japan Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi also said US President Donald Trump shared concerns about the yen’s weakness when they met last week.

“It looks like the market is coming round to the view that policy could be changing to be more yen-supportive,” said Moh Siong Sim, a strategist at Oversea-Chinese Banking Corp. “The yen has been firm since the start of the week after Trump expressed concern over the weak yen.”

Speculation is growing that the Bank of Japan could raise interest rates again as early as next month, following its decision earlier this month to lift the benchmark rate to 1.25%. The yen has strengthened about 3.5% so far this quarter after Tokyo and Washington in July conducted their first joint intervention in 15 years to prop up the currency.

Shinya Koike, section manager of the global markets trading department at Sumitomo Mitsui Trust Bank, said that quarter-end flows may be behind the yen’s rise. Currency traders also said that the move is primarily due to month- and quarter-end flows.

See also: Dollar’s best rally since March has legs as fortunes shift

The yen’s month-to-date rise of 2.33% is the most since April 2025 on a trade-weighted basis, according to the Bank of Japan’s nominal effective exchange rate index.

title: DeepSeek unveils Huawei AI chip tools that may replace Nvidia’s
article:
(Sept 30): DeepSeek has publicly released software it created with Huawei Technologies Co to programme artificial intelligence (AI) chips, showcasing its close partnership with the Chinese company working to develop technologies to replace Nvidia Corp.

The AI lab is making its software toolkit for Huawei’s Ascend accelerators open-source and free to download, the start-up said on its WeChat account on Wednesday. Those tools include TileLang, China’s answer to Nvidia’s CUDA: a software platform considered the global standard for developing AI.

The move reflects deepening ties between two of China’s leading AI firms, among a handful of players trying to fulfill Beijing’s vision of replacing American software and circuitry with local equivalents. While DeepSeek is developing open-weight models to compete with the likes of Anthropic and OpenAI, Huawei is leading China’s effort to produce the accelerators essential to data centres.

DeepSeek has actively adopted domestic chips, even though model training worldwide still relies heavily on semiconductors from Nvidia. The Chinese start-up plans to deploy at least 160,000 of Huawei’s most powerful accelerators in a massive data centre it’s building in Inner Mongolia, Bloomberg News reported last month. It’s also finalising a round of fundraising at a valuation close to CNY500 billion (US$74 billion or $95 billion), ahead of a public listing as early as this year.

A sophisticated programming language with a simple coding process is essential for building an effective AI ecosystem, DeepSeek said in its WeChat post. The company has worked with Huawei to optimise performance on Ascend 950 chips, the start-up added.

See also: Trump backs independent AI audits in shift of safety posture

Huawei provided “unreserved and vigorous support” during the research and development of the software and the two will collaborate on more innovations, DeepSeek said.

title: Singapore power rates to fall from record after fuel price drop
article:
(Sept 30): Power rates for Singapore households will decline from a record high as lower fuel costs provide some relief from inflation.

The charge will fall 10% to 28.59 Singapore cents (US$0.22) per kilowatt-hour for the three months from October, grid operator SP Group said in a statement. Singapore relies largely on imports of natural gas to generate electricity, and the authorities adjust tariffs each quarter based on prices over the first two-and-a-half months of the prior period.

While global oil and gas prices have been increasing over the last few weeks, they were generally lower during the July to mid-September period compared to when the Iran war began. Singapore’s liquefied natural gas imports are typically priced against oil for medium- and long-term contracts, or against spot LNG benchmarks.

This is set to benefit Singaporean consumers at a time when the Middle East conflict risks increasing the price of everything from gasoline to groceries. Singapore inflation accelerated for a third month to the highest in almost two years in August.

Still, the recent rebound in fuel prices amid persistent tensions in the Middle East could push electricity costs higher again next year, SP Group warned.

See also: You don’t need deep pockets to survive in F&B

“Global fuel prices have risen since September 2026 due to escalating tensions in the Middle East,” the company said in a statement. “Should this persists, electricity tariffs are expected to increase for the subsequent quarter.”

title: Trump backs independent AI audits in shift of safety posture
article:
(Sept 30): US President Donald Trump endorsed using outside auditors to assess the safety of artificial intelligence (AI) systems through an accord with Silicon Valley leaders that seeks to sidestep new government rules in addressing a groundswell of concern over AI risks.

Under the agreement forged at a White House lunch on Tuesday with nearly two dozen top tech industry executives, AI companies also committed to regularly meet to set best practices for the industry. The document carries no legal weight, though the president told reporters it is “morally binding”.

“It’s almost like a constitution, in a way,” Trump told reporters in the White House driveway following the event. “The biggest people in the world signed that, and I signed it as president, and it really is a form of protection.”

The accord emerged after a nearly two-hour meeting between the president and his guests that took place against a backdrop of rising global anxiety surrounding AI’s potentially catastrophic risks. Signers included leaders of the AI industry’s most prominent developers: Anthropic PBC chief executive officer Dario Amodei, Nvidia Corp CEO Jensen Huang and SpaceXAI’s Elon Musk.

Other signers included OpenAI president Greg Brockman, Meta Platforms Inc’s Mark Zuckerberg, and Sundar Pichai, the CEO of Google parent Alphabet Inc, according to a copy posted by Trump on his Truth Social network. Several of the firms including Anthropic and OpenAI have previously committed to having independent evaluators.

Trump’s willingness to engage on safety after previously dismissing doomsday fears as “a hoax” reflects how AI has increasingly become politically charged ahead of the November elections. Trump has emerged as one of the loudest champions of unfettered AI development, putting him at odds with voters who are sceptical of the technology. More than seven in 10 voters said they prefer candidates who back stricter AI guardrails, according to a new Quinnipiac University poll.

See also: OpenAI said to target US$30 bil in funding at US$1.4 tril value

Public fears about AI’s risks have grown following a series of high-profile hacks by rogue OpenAI agents — including one that targeted an Australian government website — and recent warnings from former AI company employees that the tech poses an existential threat to humanity.

With the accord, the administration held firm to its previous insistence that AI companies are responsible for policing themselves, but the document signalled a new openness to some guardrails. It suggested that AI companies “should” implement four layers of controls and noted that “it may make sense to codify” its recommendations into law or regulation in the future.

The embrace of third-party evaluators marks a shift in the administration’s posture towards AI safety. While the industry has clamoured for using independent assessors to vet their most advanced models, Trump administration officials have regarded the groups best-suited to conduct those reviews with scepticism over their ideological leanings.

See also: AMD to buy Fei-Fei Li’s World Labs AI startup for US$8.2 bil

Ties between many safety reviewers and a movement known as effective altruism had earlier threatened to turn third-party evaluators into a non-starter with Trump. Popular in Silicon Valley, the movement’s adherents seek to ground every decision in mathematical probabilities they believe would maximise benefit for other people, and supporters generally favour slowing AI development over fears it could lead to human extinction.

Trump’s former AI czar, David Sacks, who was present at the White House lunch on Tuesday, has dismissed outside assessments as “pseudoscience”. Even so, some of the firms poised to conduct those reviews have already met with the Center for AI Standards and Innovation, a unit inside the Commerce Department, Bloomberg News previously reported.

Beyond independent evaluators, the accord recommends that companies take safety precautions by implementing internal controls for risks related to cybersecurity, biosecurity, chemical threats and unintended actions by AI models. Companies should also build an internal team to monitor those controls and designate an independent committee of the board of directors to oversee safety teams and independent audits, it says.

Despite Tuesday’s nod at safety concerns, the images of Trump ingratiating himself with the group of billionaire executives whom he called the “the most brilliant people in the world” could provide fodder for his political opponents who accuse him of being too close to the tech industry.

During his appearance with the executives in the driveway, Trump showed a change of heart toward Amodei, who has long staked out a starkly different position from the president on AI safety. The Anthropic chief’s pledge to slow cutting-edge AI development earlier this month drew a rebuke on social media from Trump, yet the vibe was different on Tuesday.

Trump said Amodei “has been fantastic” and summoned him to address reporters, leaning closer to him and admonishing him to “be careful”. Amodei, who met with the president for a private dinner on Sunday night, embraced Trump’s call to preserve the US lead in AI yet indicated that the core safety questions remain unresolved.

“The technology has very real risks,” Amodei said. “We all need to work together to make sure that we can win and we can win safely if we do this right,” he added before stepping out of the camera’s view as Trump complained about “fake news”.

title: US administration examining Boeing software glitch that risks wider fallout
article:
(Sept 30): The US Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) is working to understand the severity of a new software glitch facing Boeing Co’s best-selling 737 Max family of jets — a determination that risks disrupting aircraft deliveries and hitting the plane-maker’s bottom line.

The agency plans to convene a so-called corrective action review board (CARB) consisting of a panel of FAA experts to evaluate whether the software problem poses a “safety of flight issue”, meaning it could endanger the aircraft or the people on board.

While CARBs are a standard part of the FAA’s safety review process, the consequences could be significant depending on the outcome. Should the arrival of the Max 7 and 10 be further delayed, it would hamper Boeing’s efforts to generate free cash flow and pare down over US$45 billion ($57 billion) of debt. Together, the two aircraft represent about a quarter of Boeing’s overall commercial backlog, a sizeable chunk of yet-to-be-realised cash.

The board will decide whether an unsafe condition exists and what actions, if any, are required. In serious situations where the FAA determines an issue poses an immediate danger to pilots, crew or the flying public, the FAA can publish an emergency airworthiness directive laying out corrective actions for aircraft owners and operators to take.

The FAA hasn’t yet said when it will convene the CARB or how long it will be before a final conclusion is reached. The European Aviation Safety Agency said it is monitoring the situation and is prepared to act accordingly, but won’t participate in the CARB directly.

Investors are meanwhile seeking to parse the impact of the agency’s review. Until the software glitch was revealed over the weekend, Boeing looked poised to gain certification for the long-delayed Max 10, with the final nod only days or a few weeks away.

See also: Airbus freighter takes first flight to challenge Boeing’s 777

The smaller Max 7 variant was certified in August. But the 737-10 in particular, the largest of the popular narrowbody family, is crucial for Boeing with orders already exceeding 1,500 aircraft, and arch-rival Airbus SE gaining more ground with its stretched A321neo models.

Boeing stock fell 6.9% in trading on Monday following the revelation that the regulator would delay certification of the Max 10.

RBC Capital Markets analyst Ken Herbert said he sees “incremental risk” to Boeing’s 2026 free cash guideline of US$1 billion to US$3 billion, which Boeing chief financial officer Jay Malave had already warned this month could be “a little bit less likely” to exceed US$2 billion as deliveries lag.

See also: SIA Engineering and Rolls Royce JV SAESL eyes growth as MRO market expands to US$120 bil

Some of Boeing’s customers struck a more optimistic tone. Ryanair Holdings plc’s chief executive officer Michael O’Leary, Boeing’s biggest operator in Europe, said on Tuesday that he didn’t think the issue is significant or would cause a substantial delay. Similarly, Alaska Air Group Inc CEO Ben Minicucci said on CNBC on Tuesday that he wasn’t “overly concerned”.

Financial risk aside, chief for Boeing is the potential reputational fallout. The company has been working to rebuild trust with the public and regulators following two fatal crashes of its 737 Max aircraft and widespread manufacturing and quality lapses uncovered after a door-sized panel blew off one of the jets in 2024.

Bank of America Corp analyst Ronald Epstein predicted that the FAA delay could span six to nine months as the agency investigates the software issue, estimating a potential US$500 million to US$750 million hit to free cash flow.

“The financial impact is manageable for Boeing, but the reputational damage brought about by the 737-Max crisis represents an enduring uphill battle even for issues of a much smaller magnitude,” Epstein said in a note.

The public disclosure of the software glitch comes at an particularly inopportune time for Boeing. The company is working to avert a potentially costly strike of its Seattle-area technicians and engineers, many of whom may work directly on these kinds of issues.

Boeing in August notified all 737 operators about the software problem, which can cause an automated navigation feature to fail during specific landing scenarios. The company said the glitch can occur when a pilot needs to abort a landing attempt, forcing the autopilot into a simpler level of automation for pitch control, which increases pilot workload compared to the standard mode used.

A representative for GE Aerospace, which supplies the affected software, said the company is “working closely with Boeing and will support the FAA’s evaluation”.

To stay ahead of Singapore and the region’s corporate and economic trends, click here for Latest Section

The software issue drew quick comparisons to the faulty flight control software, known as the Maneuvering Characteristics Augmentation System — or MCAS — that gained notoriety after it was linked to the 2018 and 2019 fatal Max crashes.

Yet officials have been quick to differentiate between the two issues.

FAA administrator Bryan Bedford told reporters on Monday that unlike with the MCAS, the pilots “remain in control of the airplane”. He said with this latest issue, the question is really how much extra work the glitch puts on pilots and “how we feel about that”, he said.

Bedford said the agency still hasn’t determined whether there’s a safety of flight issue but that it will be delaying certification of the 737 Max 10 until the FAA makes that call.

title: OpenAI said to target US$30 bil in funding at US$1.4 tril value
article:
(Sept 30): OpenAI aims to raise at least US$30 billion ($38 billion) from investors in a new round of funding, according to people familiar with the matter, after the artificial intelligence (AI) start-up pushed back its plans for an initial public offering (IPO).

The company is seeking a valuation of around US$1.4 trillion, not including the money raised, said the people, potentially vaulting it back above long-time rival Anthropic’s most recent private market valuation. Bloomberg News previously reported OpenAI was mulling a new round at a US$1.2 trillion valuation.

The fundraising discussions are early and could change, said the people, who spoke on condition of anonymity as the information is not public. The demand for the round is being led by investors, one person said, as the firm sees strong revenue growth. OpenAI declined to comment.

The ChatGPT maker has been locked in a heated battle with Anthropic to sign up more business customers and bolster revenue ahead of their planned Wall Street debuts. Both firms have filed confidential paperwork to go public, with Anthropic expected to hold its public listing as soon as this fall.

OpenAI chief executive officer Sam Altman recently said his firm would refrain from going public this year. In an interview with Bloomberg TV on Tuesday, he said the company wants to navigate a period of heightened AI safety concerns without the pressure of being a newly public company.

The ChatGPT maker is currently “adjusting” to a “new level” of AI capability and the added safety requirements that coincide with it, Altman said.

See also: AMD to buy Fei-Fei Li’s World Labs AI startup for US$8.2 bil

“We just want to get our feet under us and make sure we understand how to operate in this new way, [and] be able to make some of these decisions in front of us without the pressure of being a newly public company,” Altman said, adding that he believes investors will be “patient” with its IPO planning.

The latest fundraise is meant to serve as a bridge round to provide OpenAI with additional capital in place of an IPO, the people said. OpenAI most recently raised US$122 billion in March at a US$852 billion valuation, including the money.

Like its peers, OpenAI has faced mounting scrutiny over the potential for AI to cause catastrophic harm, including through cybersecurity breaches. OpenAI’s technology has been involved in a number of security incidents, including targeting Australian government websites. The company also said this week it would not release its latest model, GPT-6.1 Astra, because the system didn’t meet its internal safety standards.

See also: China may let Alibaba buy Nvidia’s RTX chips, Information reports

Altman has endorsed a plan by Anthropic’s Dario Amodei to slow down development of the most cutting-edge AI models and bring on independent evaluators to help safeguard the technology.

At the same time, OpenAI continues to compete aggressively in the increasingly crowded market for AI agents that field more complex tasks for users. At the company’s developer event on Tuesday, OpenAI unveiled a new always-on AI agent called Dots that is poised to compete directly with products like Muse from Meta Platforms Inc.

OpenAI is also shaking up its subscription offerings by debuting a new high-end US$500 paid tier with higher usage limits and faster processing speeds, and reducing certain usage limits for its US$200 plan.

Widely considered to be on the backfoot for much of the year, OpenAI has worked to narrow its product focus and seen renewed momentum for tools that streamline the process of coding, among other work.

OpenAI’s revenue run rate accelerated over the summer and topped US$40 billion, Bloomberg News reported in August. The company’s run rate revenue has grown by 70% since July, one person said.

title: Paramount said to draw US$109 bil of demand for high-grade bond deal
article:
(Sept 30): Paramount Skydance Corp has attracted demand more than three times the expected size of its blue-chip bond offering to help fund its acquisition of Warner Bros Discovery, as banks look to wrap up the long-awaited buyout financing.

Investors had placed more than US$109 billion ($139 billion) of orders for the deal when the books closed on Tuesday afternoon, or 3.6 times the amount expected to be sold after lenders shifted part of the funding to loans, according to people familiar with the matter. That compares with an average of four times the deal size for investment-grade bond transactions in the currency so far this year, according to data compiled by Bloomberg.

The Paramount high-grade debt offering — the largest portion of a US$52 billion financing package that also includes junk bonds and loans — stands out in a year when hyperscalers have dominated the market with jumbo sales to finance the artificial intelligence infrastructure build-out.

The US media giant has trimmed the size of the planned sale by US$2 billion to US$30 billion, while boosting the size of the loan portion of the deal by the same amount, the people said, asking not to be identified because they’re not allowed to speak publicly. It is offering first-lien US dollar-denominated bonds in eight tranches, with maturities ranging from two to 40 years.

Initial price talk for the longest-dated note, due in 2066, is a spread of about 3.65 percentage points above Treasuries, one of the people said. Apollo Global Management Inc, Bank of America Corp and Citigroup Inc are leading the offering, which is expected to price on Wednesday, the person added.

Paramount, Apollo and the banks involved in the transaction either declined or didn’t respond to requests for comments.

See also: Thailand eyes pivot to short-term debt as bond volatility rises

The debt is coming to market after a months-long delay and at a higher cost for Paramount, as a surge in Treasury yields has raised borrowing costs for companies. The bonds and loans were initially expected to be sold around mid-year, but the financing was put on hold after the Warner deal faced litigation until two settlements last week cleared the way for the offering.

Warner Brothers was the object of a bidding war earlier this year, with Paramount eventually beating out Netflix Inc in a US$110 billion transaction to create one of the world’s largest entertainment empires. Apollo, Bank of America and Citigroup provided the initial financing for the Warner acquisition, before selling down the debt to a group of 18 banks.

The financing package includes about US$12.4 billion-equivalent of junk bonds across US dollars and euros, as well as US$7.5 billion-equivalent of loans in both currencies. Both offerings are underway, with investors having placed orders of about US$15.6 billion for the high-yield notes and US$11.5 billion for the loans, according to people familiar with the matter.

See also: UK set to pay highest yield since 1999 at 10-year bond auction

The investment-grade bond market has seen a flurry of deals in recent weeks to help fund mergers and acquisitions. In the latest major offering, Sysco Corp last week raised about US$17 billion through notes sold in three currencies.

Paramount’s proposed first-lien notes received investment-grade ratings by Fitch Ratings and S&P Global Ratings, while Moody’s Ratings placed the debt one step below that level.

The Warner acquisition will increase Paramount’s debt by more than US$30 billion, pushing its leverage to about seven times a measure of earnings, according to Moody’s.

“Credit metrics at closing will therefore resemble those of highly speculative issuers with very low single-B ratings,” it said in a Monday note to clients. “High leverage, concentrated ownership, plans to prime existing senior unsecured bondholders and management’s mixed track record in meeting financial targets reflect significant governance risk,” Moody’s added.

S&P said that its BBB- rating on the first-lien debt reflects the commitment by the Ellison family — who controls Paramount — to slash leverage to 3.75 times a measure of earnings by 2028 and three times in 2029.

title: GIC acquires 16 Marriott-run hotels in Japan amid tourism boom — Bloomberg
article:
(Sept 30): Singapore’s sovereign wealth fund GIC Pte Ltd has acquired 16 hotels in Japan operated by Marriott International Inc for about ¥125 billion (US$800 million or $1.02 billion), according to people familiar with the matter.

In the latest big real estate deal in Japan, GIC took over Four Points Flex by Sheraton, a mid-price-range hotel chain, according to the people.

US investment firm KKR & Co said on Sept 25 that it sold Four Points Flex by Sheraton. It didn’t provide details such as the buyer and sale price. The chain is operating in 11 cities, including the tourist hotspots Tokyo, Osaka, Kyoto and Fukuoka.

Spokespeople for GIC and KKR declined to comment.

The weak yen has benefited the hotel business by making Japan a more affordable travel destination. The number of foreign visitors to the nation broke above 40 million for the first time last year, reaching around 42.7 million people, according to land ministry data.

Hotels are considered less vulnerable to inflation than other real estate assets as they can easily raise room rates in response to swelling expenses and stronger demand. That helps hotels maintain profitability even during periods of increases in the cost of living, like Japan is experiencing now.

See also: Temasek buys minority stake in Italian PE firm FSI

GIC’s hotel purchase follows other big Japanese real estate transactions in recent years, such as a US$900 million ($1.15 billion) acquisition of 27 resort hotels owned by Daiwa House Industry Co by a foreign investor group in 2023. Japan Hotel REIT Investment Corp’s takeover in March this year of the Hyatt Regency Tokyo hotel for ¥126 billion is another example.

KKR bought 14 hotels in 2024 from Unizo Holdings Co, which filed for a court-supervised restructuring in April 2023 due to an inability to repay bonds that were coming due.

title: Apple will sell six million iPhone Duos in 2026, Counterpoint says
article:
(Sept 30): Apple Inc is set to sell about six million units of the iPhone Duo this year, Counterpoint Research said, offering the first estimate for how the company’s inaugural foldable device will fare.

The figure, more typical of the niche foldable segment than Apple’s usual smartphone sales, is contingent on how well the company ramps up production of the new hardware, Counterpoint senior analyst Ivan Lam said. Priced at US$1,999 and set for an October release, the iPhone Duo sits atop the Apple lineup and carries industry-wide hopes for stoking greater interest and sales of foldables.

Market researcher IDC estimates foldables will grow 13% to 22.9 million units shipped this year with Apple’s help. Without the iPhone Duo, the segment would have seen a decline, it said.

Introduced alongside the Duo this month, Apple’s iPhone 18 Pro family has gotten off to a fast start in China, Counterpoint said. The company’s Pro edition smartphones were for the first time released without a corresponding base-model upgrade, steering consumers looking for an upgrade to the pricier models and helping deliver a 12% rise compared to the iPhone 17 Pro’s initial sales. That performance bucked a broad downtrend in the world’s largest smartphone market, with Chinese brands taking the brunt of a 17% year-on-year decline across this summer, according to the researchers.

That helped Apple grab 33% of China’s highly competitive smartphone arena, an unusual feat when companies like Huawei Technologies Co, Oppo, Vivo and Xiaomi Corp usually have roughly equal shares with Apple. But elevated component costs are forcing all phone makers to raise prices and try to make up the shortfall of unit sales in higher revenue per unit. That works in Apple’s favour by narrowing the cost advantage of its rivals.

“Price hikes of over US$200 on many Chinese flagship models may have raised the price anchor, strengthening the iPhone’s relative value proposition,” Lam said.

See also: AI faces US$6 tril test to justify data centres, Bain says
